summary: Describes additions to ARP that let a station ask for the protocol address that goes with a known hardware address, the reverse of normal ARP. It is mainly used on links such as Frame Relay. It was replaced by RFC 2390.

plainLanguage.summary: Normal ARP asks, who has this address? Inverse ARP asks the opposite: I know who you are on the wire, so what is your Internet address?

questions: how does inarp work on frame relay
when do you use inverse arp instead of regular arp
subtitle: Extensions to ARP that discover protocol addresses from known hardware addresses.

tldr.problem: In some networks like Frame Relay, a station knows the hardware address (DLCI) of another station but does not know its protocol address (like IP), and needs a way to discover it.
tldr.mechanism: Inverse ARP (InARP) extends the standard ARP protocol by allowing a station with a known hardware address to send a request asking for the protocol address of the target. The target responds with its protocol address, completing the address mapping.
tldr.outcome: This enables dynamic address discovery on networks like Frame Relay without requiring manual configuration. InARP was replaced by RFC 2390 with better handling of multi-addressed hosts.

today: RFC 2390 replaces this document with improved handling of multi-addressed hosts and additional operational guidance for Inverse ARP.

sections.title: What Is Inverse ARP
sections.content:
Inverse Address Resolution Protocol (InARP) is an extension of the standard ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) that solves a different problem. While ARP discovers the hardware address corresponding to a protocol address, InARP discovers the protocol address corresponding to a hardware address.

InARP is particularly useful on Frame Relay networks, where stations may have a Data Link Connection Identifier (DLCI)—a Frame Relay hardware address—associated with an established Permanent Virtual Circuit (PVC), but do not know the protocol address (such as an IP address) of the station on the other side of the connection. InARP allows dynamic discovery of this protocol address, avoiding the need for manual configuration on new virtual circuits.
sections.plainLanguage: InARP is a way to ask another computer: "I know how to reach you, but what is your Internet address?" It works by sending a question on the wire and waiting for the answer.

sections.title: The Problem: Frame Relay Address Discovery
sections.content:
Frame Relay networks identify virtual circuits using DLCIs (Data Link Connection Identifiers), which are hardware addresses. When the network announces a new virtual circuit with its DLCI, the station receiving the announcement learns of the connection but does not receive the protocol address information needed to communicate.

Alternative approaches were considered. Reverse ARP (RARP), for example, responds with the requester's protocol address, not the target's, so it was unsuitable. IP-specific mechanisms would have been limiting for networks that use multiple protocol types.

InARP solves this by allowing a Frame Relay station to directly query another station's protocol address once a new virtual circuit is established, avoiding broadcast-based methods and eliminating the need for manual static configuration. This makes virtual circuits usable immediately upon announcement.
sections.plainLanguage: When Frame Relay creates a new connection, the local station knows the connection ID but not the other station's IP address. InARP asks the other side: "What is your IP?"

sections.title: Packet Format
sections.content:
Inverse ARP uses the same packet format as standard ARP. The packet contains eight fields:

ar$hrd (Hardware type, 16 bits), ar$pro (Protocol type, 16 bits), ar$hln (Hardware address length in bytes, 8 bits), ar$pln (Protocol address length in bytes, 8 bits), ar$op (Operation code, 16 bits), ar$sha (Source hardware address), ar$spa (Source protocol address), ar$tha (Target hardware address), and ar$tpa (Target protocol address).

The operation code distinguishes InARP messages: 8 = InARP request and 9 = InARP reply. These values were chosen to avoid conflict with other ARP extensions. Hardware and protocol type values are the same as those for standard ARP.

Address field lengths depend on the network environment. For example, on IP over Frame Relay, the hardware address length is 2 to 4 bytes (for the DLCI), and the protocol address length is 4 bytes (for a 32-bit IP address).
sections.plainLanguage: InARP messages look like ARP messages but use special operation codes (8 for request, 9 for reply) to identify themselves and ask for the other station's address.

sections.title: How InARP Works
sections.content:
Unlike ARP, which broadcasts requests to the entire network, InARP sends requests directly to the target station because the hardware address is already known. A requesting station formats an InARP request by filling in its own source hardware and protocol addresses, the known target hardware address, and zero-fills the target protocol address field (the value being requested). The packet is encapsulated for the network and sent directly to the target.

Upon receiving an InARP request, a station may add the requester's address mapping to its ARP cache. Importantly, the receiving station may assume that any InARP request it receives is destined for it. It formats a reply using the requester's addresses as the target addresses in the response. If the station is unable or unwilling to reply, it ignores the request.

When the requesting station receives the InARP reply, it completes the address mapping and can use the provided information. Like ARP entries, information learned via InARP may be aged or invalidated over time according to protocol rules.
sections.plainLanguage: One station sends InARP request: "Here is my address, what is yours?" The other station receives it and sends back: "My address is X." Both stations now know each other.

sections.title: Multiple Addresses on One Interface
sections.content:
Some hosts have multiple protocol addresses assigned to a single interface. When such a host receives an InARP request, it must choose which address to respond with. The receiving station should examine the protocol address in the incoming request and respond with the protocol address that corresponds to the same protocol network.

For example, if the requesting station is probing for an IP address, a multi-addressed responding station should answer with an IP address on the same subnet as the requester. If the station does not have an appropriate address for the request, it should not respond. In the IP example, if the receiving station lacks an IP address on the requested subnet, it would not reply to that InARP request.

A multi-addressed host may send multiple InARP requests, one for each of its addresses on a given interface. However, the receiving side may answer some, all, or none of the requests depending on its configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: If a computer has multiple addresses, it picks the one that belongs to the same group as the requester's address, so they can talk to each other.

sections.title: InARP on Frame Relay Networks
sections.content:
InARP is especially useful when a new Frame Relay virtual circuit is announced. The Frame Relay station may format an InARP request addressed to the new virtual circuit. If the other side supports InARP, it returns a reply indicating the requested protocol address.

For an InARP request on Frame Relay, the operation code is 8, the hardware type is 0x000F (assigned to Frame Relay), the protocol type is the protocol being sought (such as 0x0800 for IP), and the hardware and protocol address lengths match the environment. The source hardware address is the Q.922 address of the requesting station, and the target hardware address is the Q.922 address of the newly announced virtual circuit. The target protocol address field (which the request is trying to fill in) is set to zero.

The InARP reply follows the same format, with operation code 9, and the sender's addresses filled in as the response. The RFC notes that Q.922 addresses should have the C/R, FECN, BECN, and DE bits all set to zero in InARP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: On Frame Relay, when a new connection appears, the station sends InARP to ask: "You just connected to me, what is your IP address?" The other station replies with its IP address.
